Introduction:
The COVID-19 pandemic had substantial acute impacts worldwide, with more than 7 million deaths reported to the World Health Organization by December 2024 [ 1 ]. Mortality was particularly high in Brazil, representing 9.9% of all deaths worldwide in a country that accounts for 2.7% of the world’s population. This was due to a combination of unscientific political decisions, poor central coordination as different states and regions adopted variable approaches to prevention and case management, and conflicting public messages [ 2 ].

EPICOVID-19, a population-based serological survey carried out in four different waves during 2020 with a total of over 130 000 interviews in 133 Brazilian cities, showed that individuals with lower socioeconomic conditions, lower education, indigenous ethnicity, and black or brown skin colour were more likely to present antibodies against COVID-19 [ 3 ]. Other studies reported similar patterns in both high and low/middle-income countries [ 4 , 5 ].

Economic and social disruption due to the pandemic have profoundly impacted social, health, and economic outcomes among families, such as income reduction, unemployment, interruption of studies, and food insecurity [ 6 , 7 ]. During the pandemic, a six-country study (China, Japan, Italy, South Korea, UK, and USA) reported stronger impacts among individuals with low socioeconomic status [ 8 ]. In a systematic review, including studies from 27 countries, higher rates of dropouts and failures were reported among students from lower socioeconomic positions [ 9 ].

We aimed to describe how families were impacted by the pandemic in terms of income, employment, school attendance, food insecurity, and death of family members in a nationwide Brazilian population-based sample. Impact measures were stratified by socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, including indicators socioeconomic position and ethnicity. The rationale for stratification is provided by the importance of social determinants of health globally [ 10 ] and particularly in Brazil, which is one the most highly unequal countries in the world [ 11 ]. Our hypothesis was that the pandemic had a greater impact on population groups that were already more vulnerable at its onset, such as low-income families and households headed by women.
Methods:
### Participants

Using the same sampling design as in the original 2020 study, 133 sentinel cities were selected throughout the country. The cities included Brasilia, 26 state capitals, and the largest cities in each of the country’s intermediate regions, as defined by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) [ 12 ]. In each city, a sample of 25 urban census tracts was drawn with a probability of selection proportionate to size, and 10 households were randomly selected in each tract. In each sampled household, all residents were listed, and one was randomly selected to be interviewed. If the sampled individual refused to be interviewed, a second one was sampled. If this individual also refused, the next household to the right was selected. A total of 33 250 participants were interviewed. Further details on the study methods have been described elsewhere [ 13 ]. Data were collected during May and June 2024.

### Outcomes

The following impact outcomes during the pandemic were studied: death of a family member due to COVID-19; decrease in family income; impact on work of a family member, defined as job loss (for those formally employed) or stopping working (for those in the informal sector); and impact on education, defined as any family member who stopped studying during the pandemic (analyses restricted to families with children or adolescents aged under 18). These three impact indicators referred to events or changes taking place during the pandemic. Household food insecurity during the pandemic was investigated using the Brazilian Food Insecurity Scale [ 14 ], which defines food insecurity at the household as one or more positive answers to eight questions. In addition, we analysed whether any household member had gone an entire day without eating due to lack of food. Food insecurity was assessed during the pandemic, rather than changes in food security compared to the pre-pandemic period.

### Procedures

The sampled individuals were invited to participate in the survey and informed about the objectives of the study, as well as its risks and advantages. Interviews were conducted only after the participant signed the free and informed consent form. The form was read when the selected individual was under 18 years of age; in this case, the child or adolescent either signed or fingerprinted the form, which a legal guardian also signed. The study represented minimal risk to health, being restricted to the application of a short questionnaire. Participants were informed that they could stop participating at any time during data collection.

### Data analysis

We used Stata 15 for the analyses. The prevalence of each outcome was described according to sociodemographic characteristics of the families, including region of the country, number and age distribution of family members, whether the family was headed by a woman, highest educational level of a family member, monthly family income, household wealth, and race/skin colour of the interviewee.

Household wealth was calculated through an index based on principal component analysis (PCA) of a set of household characteristics and assets (computer, internet access, colour television, air conditioning, motor vehicles, cable television, number of bathrooms, and number of residents per bedroom), similar to what is done for Demographic and Health surveys [ 15 ]. The first component of the PCA explained 37.8% of the total variance, and all variables had factor loadings above 0.4, except for internet access (0.24) and cable television (0.35). The wealth index was moderately correlated with reported monthly family income (Pearson’s correlation coefficient of 0.62), and both variables were retained in the analyses.

Information on race/skin colour—the official variable employed by the Brazilian classification—was not collected on each family member but only for the respondent. In consonance with the official classification used in Brazilian studies, the categories included (in Portuguese): branco, preto, pardo, amarelo, or indigenous; respectively white, black, brown, Asian, and indigenous [ 16 ]. Family income in the month preceding the interview was expressed in Brazilian minimum wages (∼US$250).

Proportions were compared using the Wald test. Prevalence ratios were estimated using Poisson regression. Sampling weights were employed to account for the sampling design (by using the ‘svyset’ command) and to reproduce the characteristics of the pooled set of 133 cities in terms of population size, sex, age, and race/colour, using the 2022 Census results [ 17 ]. All findings reported below resulted from the weighted analyses. Further details on weights are available elsewhere [ 18 ].

Equiplot graphs [ 19 ] were used to show inequalities in the outcomes according to wealth quintiles. The slope index of inequality (SII) was used to estimate the magnitude of income-related disparities [ 20 ]. The index ranges from −1 to +1, with negative values indicating higher levels of the outcome among the poor and positive values indicating the opposite.
Results:
Interviews were carried out in 33 250 households. Table 1 presents the distribution of households according to socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. Most households had a member with at least 9 years of schooling, a family income of up to three minimum wages, and were headed by a male.

Table 2 presents the five impact outcomes according to region, age, sex, wealth index, income, and race/skin colour. The death of a family member due to COVID-19 was reported in 14.7% [95% confidence interval (CI): 13.8%; 15.6%] of all households, being more common in wealthier and more educated families and in the North and Central-West regions. Reduced family income during the pandemic was observed in 48.6% (95% CI: 47.1%; 50.1%) of the households, with the highest prevalence in the North and Northeast and among families with current incomes of one minimum wage or less. About one of every three participants [34.9% (95% CI: 33.4%; 36.4%)] reported that they or someone in their household had lost their job or stopped working during the COVID-19 outbreak, this being more frequent in families whose income was three minimum wages or less. Concerning school attendance, 21.5% (95% CI: 20.1%; 22.9%) stated that a family member interrupted their studies during the pandemic. Food insecurity during the outbreak was reported in 47.4% (95% CI: 45.9%; 48.8%) of the families, and in 8.5% (95% CI: 7.7; 9.3), at least one adult failed to eat on one or more days due to lack of money (data not shown in Table). Food insecurity, work disruptions, and interruption of studies were more common among families earning one minimum wage or less, those led by women, and households with six or more residents. In contrast, white subjects were less likely to report food insecurity. Race/skin colour was not associated with the remaining outcomes. Table 3 describes outcomes according to race/skin colour stratified by family income.

Figure 1 shows that the widest absolute wealth inequality was observed for food insecurity, where prevalence in the poorest quintile was more than 30 percentage points higher than in the wealthiest quintile. For the death of a family member, the slope index of inequality (SII) was positive [0.08 (95% CI: 0.07; 0.10)], whereas for loss of income [SII: −0.16 (95% CI: −0.18 to −0.14)], impact on work [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.11 to −0.07)], school disruption [SII: −0.09 (95% CI: −0.12 to −0.06)], and food insecurity [SII: −0.42 (95% CI: −0.43 to −0.4)], the slope index of inequality was negative, indicating greater disadvantage among the poorest. The lower SII estimate for food insecurity indicates that absolute wealth inequality was higher for food insecurity.
Discussion:
Our large nationwide, population-based survey in Brazil documented important impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, 4 years after the initial cases in 2020. The impact included high frequencies of family deaths, income reductions, food insecurity, work, and schooling disruptions. The stronger impacts tended to affect already vulnerable groups, as discussed below.

The literature extensively documents the pandemic’s impacts on income, work, and schooling [ 21 ]. Our findings quantify the magnitude of such impacts in Brazil, as well as confirm the importance of disparities associated with region of residence, educational levels, income, wealth, gender, family composition, and ethnicity. In sequence, we discuss in greater detail our findings on food insecurity, family composition, and regional disparities, as well as on the apparently paradoxical inequalities in mortality at the household level.

Food insecurity was particularly frequent in low-income and female-headed families, those with six or more members and with children, and among indigenous populations. Almost two-thirds of the low-income families reported food insecurity; the SII value of 0.42 indicates a wide prevalence gap of 42 percentage points between the poorest and wealthiest households. Due to our cross-sectional design, we cannot assert that the reported levels of food insecurity were fully attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic, because such shortages might have predated the arrival of the virus in the country. Nevertheless, the literature suggests that insecurity increased during the pandemic. A United Nations report published in 2020 showed increases in global food insecurity, with particularly severe effects in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This was attributed to increased unemployment, loss of income, and disruptions in supply chains [ 22 ]. In Latin America, a cohort study in Mexico showed increased food insecurity from 41.6% before the pandemic to 53.8% during the pandemic period [ 23 ]. In Brazil, the impact was amplified by pre-existing inequalities, with the most vulnerable families facing rising rates of food insecurity and undernutrition. Food insecurity was also attributed to the ineffectiveness of social policies during the crisis, leaving millions at risk of hunger and extreme poverty [ 24 ]. Food insecurity may have long-lasting effects, as affected individuals may be more likely to suffer from post-COVID conditions, as reported in a Brazilian cohort study [ 25 ].

There were important regional differences within Brazil. The North (Amazon) and Northeast regions were the most affected by reductions in income, interruption of studies, and food insecurity. These two regions were affected by the pandemic’s fastest initial escalation in Brazil. In our original EPICOVID-19 survey carried out in 2020, the highest prevalence of antibodies against SARS-Cov-2 was initially observed in 11 cities along the Amazon River, after which prevalence increased rapidly in the Northeast [ 26 ]. In addition to the well-documented socioeconomic disparities among the Brazilian regions [ 27 ], factors such as the structure and organization of health systems and management of the pandemic may have played a role. Race/skin colour may also have played a role, as indigenous people—who are concentrated in the Amazon area—were amongst those with the highest levels of infection, hospitalization, and deaths during the pandemic, accentuating their pre-existing vulnerability to acute respiratory diseases, even before the pandemic [ 28 ].

Earlier studies showed that the North region also had the highest case fatality among all five regions of Brazil, both in indigenous and non-indigenous people [ 28–30 ]. Baqui et al . [ 31 ] hypothesize that the regional effect is driven by the increased burden of pre-existing comorbidity in the poorest regions and among the indigenous, leading to increased COVID-19 susceptibility and severity, compounded by unequal access to health care, including intensive care. We also investigated gender-related issues. Because impact outcomes were measured at the household level, it did not make sense to break them down according to the sex of the randomly chosen survey respondent. Instead, we examined gender inequality by comparing families according to the sex of the head of the household. Families headed by women, which represented 40% of the sample, were disproportionately affected by higher rates of food insecurity, income reduction, and interruption of studies. These findings were consistent with those of other studies worldwide that reported on individual-level outcomes. Women were more likely than men to experience negative work outcomes, such as permanent job loss and reduced income, or reductions in total hours worked, both for paid and unpaid work, thus aggravating pre-existing gender gaps [ 32–36 ]. Increased childcare needs due to school interruptions were also reported to impact women’s work. Regarding food insecurity during the pandemic, an Ethiopian study also reported higher levels in female-headed households [ 37 ]. A systematic review focused on pregnant women from different countries found that food insecurity during the pandemic ranged from 11% to over 80% [ 38 ], while a survey in the Amazon Region reported a prevalence of food insecurity of 57% also among pregnant women, with higher levels in large families and in low-income households [ 39 ]. Our findings also showed increased risks in large families for income reduction, work and schooling disruptions, and food insecurity.

Taken together, our findings suggest that pre-existing disparities exacerbated the impacts of the pandemic and likely affected subsequent recovery in terms of food security, education, income, and employment. In many LMICs, households have turned to agricultural work to compensate for job losses in the services sector, and informal work has substantially increased among the poorest [ 7 ]. As an upper-middle-income country, Brazil’s GDP fell 3.3% in 2020, which represented a record low annual decline in recent history. On the positive side, this decline was reversed after the pandemic [ 17 ].

Similar impacts on inequality were seen in some high-income countries, like UK [ 40 ] and Korea [ 41 ], where the pandemic accentuated socioeconomic disparities, especially affecting low-income workers and other vulnerable groups. Lastly, the interruptions in schooling may also aggravate inequalities and social exclusion [ 9 , 42 ].

We found that deaths of family members were more commonly reported in wealthier and more educated families. This finding persisted even after adjusting for sex, age, region, and skin colour. This was a surprising finding as—despite having universal healthcare—poor Brazilians still have lower access to complex health services and shorter life expectancies than their better-off counterparts [ 43 ]. Our finding also contradicts the Brazilian literature on the relationship between COVID-19 mortality and socioeconomic factors, which is mostly based on ecological studies correlating routinely collected mortality data with census-based economic indicators. Most such studies found higher mortality in poorer or more deprived areas of the country [ 31 , 44–48 ]. However, we were unable to find any individual-level study from Brazil on this association. Two observations may help explain our paradoxical findings. First, due to differential life expectancy according to socioeconomic position, wealthier families were more likely than poor households to include elderly members before the pandemic, and these persons were at the highest risk of COVID-19 death. Our current post-pandemic analyses showed that 37% of all households in the poorest quintile and 46% of those in the wealthiest quintile had at least one member aged 60 or older. Similarly, these proportions were 35% and 45% for family income brackets below 1 and over 5 minimum wages ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Such variability in age composition helps explain why wealthier households were more likely to report a death from a disease that primarily killed elderly people. Further analyses also showed that the sharpest socioeconomic increases in mortality were observed for the deaths of the parents of the respondents than for younger relatives (Supplementary Table S2). Another possible explanation is the higher prevalence of non-communicable diseases among the poorest [ 49 ], which may have led them to attribute COVID-19-related deaths to other pre-existing conditions.

Our study’s strengths include its standardized survey methodology and its large population-based sample, including over 100 cities spread throughout a country with 8.5 million km 2 . Yet, some limitations should be acknowledged. First, the time elapsed from the peak of the pandemic to the data collection date poses the risk of recall bias. However, the outcomes under study are objectively defined major events, such as death or unemployment, which reduces the likelihood of poor recall. Second, our sample was restricted to large cities that usually have better access to health care, and 15% of the national population living in rural areas were not included. Third, the higher proportion of negative outcomes in female-headed families might result from the death of a male head of household during the pandemic. For two reasons, we do not think this is a likely source of bias. We found that the proportion of households led by women in our sample was very close to that reported in the 2022 National Census [ 17 ]. In addition, reported deaths in the family did not vary according to the sex of the head of the household ( Table 2 ), and lastly, exclusion from the analyses of households where a spouse died due to COVID-19 (Supplementary Table S3) led to very similar results to those reported above. Lastly, we could not collect information from households whose members were away during the attempted visit or refused to participate.

In conclusion, substantial impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil were documented in terms of mortality, nutrition, income, work, and education. The pandemic disproportionately affected population subgroups that were already vulnerable before the pandemic, such as low-income, female-headed, and indigenous households, thus contributing to exacerbate pre-existing disparities. Our findings underscore the importance of developing and expanding targeted policies to address the needs of the most vulnerable and will contribute to their recovery. Further research should focus on effective interventions to reduce these disparities, including food security programmes, and education support for children from low-income households, and on preparedness to face future epidemics.
